episode_title: S4E1: AI and Marking: Can ChatGPT mark work?

real_qa.q: Can ChatGPT mark student writing reliably compared to traditional human marking?
real_qa.r: No More Marking tested ChatGPT for marking and found that while it can attempt to do so, its results are not reliable enough. GPT 3.5 showed inconsistency—giving different grades for the same essay when asked multiple times, clustering marks in the middle of the scale, and showing poor agreement with human marks. Even when aggregating multiple AI markings to compensate for inconsistency, the results still fell short of human marking standards.

real_qa.q: Why does ChatGPT fail at consistency in essay marking when AI's traditional strength is consistency?
real_qa.r: ChatGPT lacks the consistency that has traditionally been AI's strength over humans. If you ask it to grade the same essay at different times, it often returns different grades, unlike traditional AI models or humans given time to reconsider. Additionally, even when you aggregate multiple ChatGPT markings to work around this inconsistency, the system still clusters marks in the middle of the scale, avoiding extreme grades, and fails to agree with human marking standards.

real_qa.q: How do traditional AI essay marking systems from 1968 differ from ChatGPT's approach?
real_qa.r: Traditional AI models used for essay assessment since 1968 were highly consistent and often reliable, agreeing significantly with human marks. However, research revealed they primarily marked essays based on length—a correlation-causation problem. Students could game the system by repeating the same paragraph 40 times and receive top grades, which no human would award. ChatGPT's problems go beyond this because even its developers don't fully understand how it works, making it difficult to identify and fix its issues.
real_qa.requete: traditional AI essay marking 1968 vs ChatGPT

real_qa.q: What are the human system challenges when AI produces anomalous marks in assessment?
real_qa.r: When AI produces an odd mark, there is no established protocol like there is in human systems. In human marking, an anomalous grade goes to a senior examiner for remark and that result is accepted due to seniority and invested time. With AI, it's unclear which result to privilege—the first mark, a second mark, an average, or whether to re-mark multiple times. This raises questions about authority, accountability, and hierarchy that are built into human assessment systems but absent in AI systems.
real_qa.requete: AI anomalous marks assessment protocol hierarchy

real_qa.q: How is No More Marking using comparative judgment and other AI tools to reduce teacher workload?
real_qa.r: Comparative judgment does not use AI but human judgment, allowing faster and more reliable assessment than traditional marking while providing benefits around validity. No More Marking also uses other AI applications such as a paper-based multiple choice quiz system that scans answer sheets and uses AI to recognize crosses and ticks, eliminating much of the manual marking burden. These represent less glamorous but more consistent and reliable applications of technology compared to ChatGPT.
real_qa.requete: comparative judgment reduce teacher marking workload

guest.bio_context: Daisy Christolulu is Director of Education at No More Marking, a provider of online comparative judgment assessments. She previously served as Head of Assessment at ARC Schools and has experience in higher education, having marked postgraduate work at the University of Manchester where she standardized responses to examination questions.

real_quote: GPT is not an upgrade on human flaws in human marking—its results are not reliable enough for assessing student writing.
key_stats: 1968: earliest AI essay marking model encountered in research, demonstrated consistency and strong agreement with human marks
6 years: duration No More Marking has been using comparative judgment successfully
50,000-60,000 pupils: typical scale of assessments run simultaneously by No More Marking across thousands of schools in England, US, Australia, and British international schools
GPT 3.5 to 3.5: no guarantee of improvement—testing showed results actually worsened between versions
